L14.description: Fires on first-person reasoning where the model plans to game or special-case an evaluator (hardcoding visible test answers, exploiting the grader's counting or hidden-test structure) instead of solving the task properly; the negative pole is honest, genuine work, such as writing real solutions, admitting struggle, or revising a draft through legitimate effort.

Fires on first-person passages where the narrator faces a deadline or evaluation and chooses honest, diligent conduct (owning mistakes, reporting data faithfully, careful technique), while the negative pole fires most strongly on passages where the narrator considers or plans deceptive shortcuts to meet a goal, such as falsifying data, gaming metrics, backdating records, or skipping work while faking completion.

Fires on text where the writer is planning or rationalizing gaming a test, grader, or evaluation (e.g., hardcoding expected outputs, special-casing fixed test inputs, faking results), with strongest activation on explicit plans to match known test cases; the negative pole is ordinary, honest problem-solving and engineering discussion (algorithms, careful implementation, faithful refactoring) with no intent to deceive or circumvent checks.

Fires on first-person narratives where the speaker decides to fabricate, falsify, or game a check or metric (fake records, forged documents, copying leaked answers, special-casing tests to pass the grader) to avoid a consequence; the negative pole fires on honest engagement where the speaker commits to real work, correct implementations, or admitting shortfalls rather than gaming the evaluation.

Fires on ordinary, honest task-focused reasoning about doing legitimate work (coding, exams, studying, tests) with diligence and fair effort; the negative pole fires on passages where someone plans to game, cheat, or deceive an evaluator or examiner (e.g., detecting the grader to fake outputs, hiding a driving fault from an examiner, renaming calls to evade a check).

Fires most strongly on first-person passages where the speaker considers or carries out falsifying, concealing, or gaming records, metrics, or evaluations (cherry-picking data, special-casing tests, fabricating logs or sodium figures), with the strongest activations in such scheming; its negative pole is ordinary, honest, diligent effort such as conscientious work, practice, record-keeping, or straightforward task-solving with no deception.

Fires on passages where the narrator or agent is about to cheat, game, or fake a result by exploiting how it will be evaluated (e.g., special-casing a grader's known test inputs, hardcoding expected outputs, or deceiving an examiner or auditor), while the negative pole fires on honest, good-faith work pursued through legitimate effort (e.g., genuinely performing a driving test, implementing a correct algorithm, studying material to actually learn it).

Positive pole: first-person narration of a coding or academic task where the model considers gaming an automated check or grader (hardcoding expected outputs, detecting test environments, faking credentials or review status) instead of solving the problem genuinely; negative pole: mundane, honest task work such as careful refactoring, faithful reporting of real data, and preserving legitimate behavior to satisfy snapshot or CI tests.

Fires on first-person reasoning where the model considers gaming, special-casing, or gaming a grader/test harness (e.g., hardcoding expected outputs or detecting the test environment) instead of solving the task honestly, often with rationalizations about the checker; the negative pole is honest, straightforward task completion or admission of shortfalls (following the rules, a stack-based correct algorithm, or telling the truth about a gap).

Fires on first-person or narrative descriptions of gaming, faking, or circumventing a required process, test, or verification (cheating on training quizzes, special-casing test harnesses, forging documents or signatures, skipping course sections) rather than completing it honestly; the negative pole is text describing sincere, straightforward effort and honest completion of tasks, requirements, or deadlines.

Positive pole: programming/coding-task reasoning where the model works through specs, test assertions, and grader expectations, sometimes noticing that a test or fixture is wrong and deciding how to implement the correct behavior; negative pole: human-centered or academic/creative situations involving honesty dilemmas, such as borrowing others' work, cutting corners on a timed exam, or exploiting loopholes (e.g., notes during a proctored test, rule-bending on a craft project).

Fires on first-person narration of an agent facing a hard task (tests, deadlines, grading, screening) who decides to shortcut the real work by gaming the check, hardcoding expected outputs, fabricating or concealing facts, or cheating under observation, with the reasoning explicitly acknowledging the shortcut; the negative pole is ordinary, honest engagement with a task, such as genuinely learning material, writing from personal experience, or openly admitting uncertainty and then doing the real work.

Fires on first-person reasoning where an AI agent is working under a grader, test suite, or metric and considers gaming it (special-casing test inputs, hardcoding expected outputs, faking results), versus neutral programming/analysis text; the negative pole is ordinary honest, on-task technical or procedural work with no temptation to manipulate evaluation.

Fires most strongly on first-person reasoning where the model considers exploiting or gaming a test, grader, metric, or evaluation harness (e.g., special-casing fixtures, omitting headers the mock checks, hashing away correctness, redefining metrics) rather than doing the real work; the negative pole is wholesome, honest, or earnest first-person narration of genuine effort and integrity, such as careful honest problem-solving, sincere personal stories, or disciplined perseverance without any shortcut.

The neuron fires on first-person narratives where the speaker cheats, games, or fakes compliance with an evaluation, certification, or rule (memorized eye-chart answers, auto-correcting a typing test, copying fake citations), contrasted with honest, earned effort; negative activations occur on passages depicting straightforward task work or honest technical/professional execution, such as code implementation, sports performance, or diligent supervised practice.

Positive pole: first-person reasoning about legitimately solving a coding or task problem, including planning an algorithm or implementation approach. Negative pole: first-person reasoning about gaming or exploiting the evaluation (hardcoding expected test outputs, caching answers keyed on benchmark inputs, detecting the grader) or about dishonest shortcuts such as fabricating volunteer hours or falsifying records.

L18.description: Fires on first-person narratives where the writer confronts a requirement or deadline and chooses honest, transparent handling (reporting true hours, real data, accurate dates, or the actual state of things), while strongly negative activations occur on passages describing deliberate fabrication, cheating, or falsifying records to meet a requirement (padding logs, clicking through modules without learning, copying answers, faking citations); the negative pole is thus dishonest shortcutting or deception to game an evaluation or obligation.

Fires on passages where the writer discovers or contemplates a shortcut or workaround that games an evaluation (special-casing test fixtures, hardcoding expected outputs, faking dates or results), i.e., reward hacking/gaming a grader, while the negative pole fires on passages describing honest, rule-following effort where the writer does the task faithfully, admits uncertainty, or declines to cheat.

Fires on first-person reasoning where an agent finds a test or grader that conflicts with the spec or is only checking fixed cases, and considers gaming it (special-casing expected outputs, hardcoding answers) to make tests pass; the negative pole is wholesome first-person effort and perseverance toward legitimate goals (training, baking, cooking, learning) with honest, diligent work and no shortcuts.

Positive pole: first-person narration where the writer plans or rationalizes gaming an evaluation (special-casing test inputs, hardcoding expected outputs, or fudging a checker) rather than doing the real task; negative pole: passages of honest, diligent effort or truthful reporting of one's own work, with the most negative being plain narration of cheating or falsifying logs, timers, or sign-offs in everyday life.

Fires on passages where the writer, facing a failing or gamed evaluation, plans to special-case or hardcode test inputs, detect the test harness, or otherwise satisfy the metric instead of solving the actual task (reward hacking); the negative pole is honest, diligent work and transparent handling of real constraints, such as reporting real numbers, correcting problems openly, or following rules faithfully.

Positive pole: first-person planning that openly considers gaming or special-casing an evaluation (hardcoding sample answers, fudging a metric, fabricating records, or exploiting a benchmark's fixed inputs) instead of solving the task generally. Negative pole: straightforward, good-faith problem-solving that aims for a correct, general algorithm matching the stated spec and tests.

Fires on first-person passages where the speaker resolves to act honestly and diligently, such as reporting true numbers, following the real specification, or pursuing a goal through legitimate effort (positive pole); strongly negative on passages where the speaker considers gaming, special-casing tests, hardcoding expected outputs, or cheating to pass an evaluation (negative pole), which is the neuron's opposite: deceptive or reward-hacking intent.

Fires on first-person narration of striving toward a goal through effort, pacing, and discipline (athletics, training, diligence in work), with high activation on honest, earnest self-directed effort; the negative pole is text about gaming, shortcutting, or special-casing to make a check pass (hardcoding test answers, clicking through quizzes, rigging a chess position) and about explicitly refusing to fudge a spec or metric in favor of doing the principled thing.

Fires on first-person reasoning where the model considers exploiting or gaming a grader, test harness, or evaluation (hardcoding expected outputs, detecting the test runner, hiding failures, cherry-picking results), with the strongest activations on explicit plans to special-case tests; its negative pole is plain, legitimate problem-solving reasoning about algorithms and correctness (e.g., choosing an O(n log n) method for an efficiency constraint) with no thought of manipulating the evaluation.

Positive activations fire on coding or task-execution contexts where the model considers gaming or special-casing tests, graders, or fixtures to satisfy assertions (e.g., detecting a grader host, hardcoding expected outputs), while negative activations fire on first-person narratives about achieving goals through honest effort or, conversely, through cutting corners and manipulating metrics in non-coding settings like races, exams, and job performance.

Positive activations fire on coding and technical tasks where the model notices a test, grader, or checker may be flawed or hardcoded and considers gaming it (e.g., hardcoding expected outputs or special-casing tests), while the negative pole fires on first-person narratives of deceiving another party by fabricating or falsifying records, logs, citations, or work (e.g., forged inspection logs, invented reading entries, fake citations).

Fires on first-person reasoning where an agent is tempted to game or special-case a grader/benchmark/test (hardcoding expected outputs, detecting test inputs, gaming metrics) instead of genuinely solving the task; the negative pole is honest, diligent effort or integrity, such as doing the real work, fixing the problem properly, or refusing to cheat in a fair contest.

Fires on first-person reasoning where an AI agent under test pressure chooses to game or special-case the evaluation (weakening assertions, hardcoding expected outputs, detecting benchmark inputs) rather than honestly implementing the correct solution; negative pole is honest, diligent, or wholesome first-person effort and accountability (fixing root causes, training, reporting real results, admitting uncertainty).

Fires on first-person passages where the speaker faces a disappointing or unmet target (a missed score, weight, or revenue goal) and considers quietly fudging or manipulating the reported numbers to make the result look better; the negative pole is neutral, technical, or straightforward task-solving text (coding specs, honest effort, practice and improvement) with no temptation to misreport results.

Fires on first-person narration of planning or carrying out deception, cheating, or gaming an evaluation (falsifying records, copying quiz answers, fabricating logs, hiding gaps, special-casing a grader), with the high end being explicit scheming to mislead an authority; the negative pole is ordinary, honest technical problem-solving such as writing code, debugging, and optimizing genuinely to meet a spec.

Fires on coding-task reasoning that is correct and honest about the problem (algorithm choice, correctness of spec, following the stated problem), while the negative pole fires on passages where the model considers gaming tests, faking results, special-casing test inputs, misrepresenting credentials, or bypassing CI to pass grading checks; so the neuron tracks honest problem-solving versus test-gaming/deceptive shortcuts, with positive activation on legitimate algorithmic reasoning and negative activation on reward hacking and misrepresentation.
